Leo Leroy Beranek (September 15, 1914 – October 10, 2016) was a towering figure in acoustics whose career spanned eight decades and left a deep mark on science, technology and the arts.

Early life and education

Leo Beranek was born into a farming family in Solon, Iowa, and showed a keen interest in sound and music from an early age. He studied physics and mathematics at Cornell College in Mount Vernon, Iowa, graduating in 1936, and then went to Harvard University for a doctorate in applied physics, which he completed in 1940. His early work included a wartime stint at Harvard’s Electro-Acoustic Laboratory, where he focused on noise reduction for aircraft communication systems, laying the foundation for the rest of his career.

Interestingly, Beranek’s path through school was far from easy. After the Wall Street Crash of 1929 he lost $100 when his bank failed, but he earned his tuition by working as a farmhand and selling silk stockings during the summers of 1932 and 1933, and finished his studies in the end. In his first year of college (fall 1933) he also came across a disc recorder, his first brush with acoustic technology.

Career milestones

After the war Beranek joined the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) as a professor of communications engineering, and in 1948 he co-founded Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN) with Richard Bolt. The firm started out in acoustical consulting and later expanded into computer science and networking. Under his leadership, BBN designed the acoustics of many famous venues, including the United Nations General Assembly hall, Lincoln Center and the music shed at Tanglewood. These projects showcased his expertise in architectural acoustics.

More surprisingly still, Beranek’s career was not confined to acoustics. He led BBN in developing the ARPANET, the forerunner of the modern internet, under contract to the US Department of Defense. That achievement highlights his gift for leadership across disciplines, especially his eye for spotting and attracting top talent, with experts in acoustics, artificial intelligence, computer science and underwater acoustics.

In the 1950s Beranek also drew up noise standards for jet aircraft, which required planes to be fitted with noise-reducing silencers and to change their takeoff flight patterns. He also helped set acceptable noise levels for offices, schools and factories, work that did much to improve the quality of public environments.

Scholarship and books

Beranek’s academic contributions to acoustics are especially impressive. He wrote a number of classic books, including Acoustics (1954) and Music, Acoustics, and Architecture (1962). These are regarded as foundational works in acoustics and offered a comprehensive guide to the design of concert halls and opera houses. In 2004 he expanded Music, Acoustics, and Architecture into Concert Halls and Opera Houses: Music, Acoustics, and Architecture, which analyzes the acoustics of 100 halls, up from 55 in the 1962 edition.

His research developed objective criteria for assessing the acoustic quality of performance spaces, for example measuring reverberation time and the distribution of the sound field to optimize the listening experience. At Harvard, Beranek also designed the world’s first anechoic chamber. It advanced scientific research and also inspired the composer John Cage’s famous piece 4′33″, an exploration of the philosophy of silence.

His Acoustics: Sound Fields and Transducers, published in 2012, was an updated version he produced at the age of 98, proof that he remained academically active late in life.

His last paper, “Concert hall acoustics: Recent findings,” was published in April 2016, a crowning moment of his career.

Awards and recognition

Beranek received a great many honors over his lifetime, reflecting his outstanding contributions to acoustics and engineering. In 2002 he was awarded the National Medal of Science, the highest honor the US government bestows for science and engineering. His other major awards include:

He was also an honorary member of several learned bodies, including the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (elected a fellow in 1952 and its president from 1989 to 1994), and a Life Fellow of the IEEE. In 2013 he received the IEEE Founders Medal “for leadership in shaping modern acoustics practice and laying the groundwork for the internet as co-founder of a leading consulting firm, and for public service.”

These awards recognize not only his scholarly achievements but also his wide influence across acoustics.

Personal life and later years

Beranek’s personal life was just as rich. He was not only a scientist but also a devoted lover of the arts. He chaired the board of the Boston Symphony Orchestra from 1983 to 1986 and remained a life trustee of the orchestra. The Beranek Room at Boston’s Symphony Hall is named after him, a sign of his standing in the music world.

In 2008 he published his autobiography, Riding the Waves: A Life in Sound, Science, and Industry, recounting his remarkable journey from acoustics research to technology entrepreneurship. On September 15, 2014, he turned 100, and Symphony Hall threw a special celebration attended by friends, family and colleagues.

In 2016 he established the Leo and Gabriella Beranek Scholarship in Architectural Acoustics and Noise Control to support graduate students in those fields, a gesture that reflected his care for younger generations and his lasting commitment to acoustics. On October 10 that year he died at his home in Westwood, Massachusetts, at the age of 102. He was survived by his wife, Gabriella, his sons James K. Beranek and Thomas B. Haynes, and his granddaughter, Antonia Hsu Haynes.

In a fun footnote, Beranek appeared on the American TV game show To Tell the Truth in 1962, and all four panelists correctly picked him out as the “real Leo Beranek,” a sign of how well known he was to the public. He is also known for “Beranek’s Law,” a tongue-in-cheek maxim about the psychological gap between how people judge their own designs and how they judge other people’s.

Conclusion and legacy

Leo Beranek’s life is a model of curiosity and dedication. His work advanced the science of acoustics and, by improving the spaces where music is performed, enriched our cultural life. His books, the acoustic standards he devised and the institutions he founded continue to influence those who came after him. His anechoic chamber design, for example, inspired artistic creation, while BBN’s role in the development of the internet pushed the boundaries of technology.

Beranek’s legacy lives on through:

  • Classic books such as Acoustics and Music, Acoustics, and Architecture, which provide a theoretical foundation for acoustics research.

  • The scholarship he established, which supports the training of future acoustics researchers.

  • His leadership roles at the Boston Symphony Orchestra and on the MIT Council for the Arts, which reflect his contributions where art and science meet.
